houserules.title: House rules: keep ALL of your work

sections.p: Your teacher grades the code you submit, so your earlier work has to stay in the box as proof. **Never delete code.** When you are done with some code, or fix it, or replace it, **comment it out** instead.

steps: Select the lines and press **Ctrl + /**. A `#` goes in front of each line, the line turns gray, Python skips it, and it stays there.
Press **Ctrl + /** again to turn it back on.

sections.p: Comment out the old version and type the new version on the line **right below** it.
Each step tells you exactly which kind to write and where. Follow it exactly.
A comment on its **OWN line**, **ABOVE** the code it names, like `# Step 3`.
A comment on its **OWN line**, directly **ABOVE** (or directly **BELOW**) the line it explains.
ex: # // rounds down, so the .5 is dropped

sections.p: A comment on the **SAME line**, **AFTER** the code, with a few spaces before the `#`.

sections.good: Do exactly what each step says. A comment that doesn't explain anything, like `#comment`, earns no credit.

commentout.title: How do I comment out everything above?

sections.p: A **comment** is a line that starts with `#`. Python skips it completely, but it stays in your code box so your teacher can see it. Commenting out your old code keeps your work and keeps your output short.

steps: Click once **inside the code box** so the blinking cursor is there.
Press **Ctrl + A**. Everything in the box turns blue (selected).
Press **Ctrl + /** (the slash key). A `#` appears at the start of every line.
Click at the very bottom of the code box and start your heading comment, like `# Step 5`.

sections.good: Only the lines that start with `#` are skipped. Your new code at the bottom (no `#`) is the only code that runs.

list: **Nothing happened?** Click inside the code box first, then try again.
**Pressed it twice by accident?** Press **Ctrl + /** again and your code turns back on. Your `# Step` headings stay as comments.
You never need to delete code. If you did delete something by mistake, type it again and comment it out.

notekinds.title: Heading, comment above, and end-of-line comment: what is the difference?

sections.p: All three are comments (they start with `#`). The only difference is **where** you put them.

sections.h: 1. Heading comment: its own line, ABOVE the code
2. Comment above (or comment below): its own line right next to the line it explains
ex: # // rounds down, so the .5 is dropped

sections.h: 3. End-of-line comment: on the SAME line, after the code

sections.warn: Leave a few spaces before the `#` on an end-of-line comment. And a comment must say something. A comment like `#comment` earns no credit because it doesn't explain anything.

sections.h: Which one does my step want?
quiz: "Add an end-of-line note at the end of each print line"
Put the `#` on the same line, after the closing bracket.
"Add a note above the first print line"
Put a new line directly above it that starts with `#`.
"Put a heading comment ABOVE the program"
A `#` line on its own, above all the lines of that program.

runit.title: How do I run my code? Where is the output?

steps: Click the orange **Run** button at the top (or press **Ctrl + Enter**).
Look at the **Output** box on the right. Everything your `print(...)` lines show appears there.
If your program asks a question with `input()`, a small box pops up. Type your answer and press OK.
Click **Clear output** to wipe the Output box so the next run is easy to read.

sections.warn: Only the code that does NOT start with `#` runs. If your output is empty, check that you didn't comment out the line you wanted to run.

readerror.title: I got a red error. What do I do?

sections.p: Errors are Python telling you exactly what it couldn't do. They are not a sign that you're bad at this. Even professional programmers see them all day.

steps: Look at the **last line** of the red message. It says the kind of error and what went wrong.
Read the **💡 What this means here** box under it. It explains the error in plain English.
Look at the line number in the message (like `Line 3`). The problem is on that line or just above it.
Fix one thing, then click Run again.
Still stuck? Re-read the step and compare each character of your code to the example.

list: A **typo** (a missing quote, a missing bracket, a capital letter in the wrong place).
A **missing colon or bracket** at the end of a line.
Using a variable that does not exist yet, or spelling it differently.

printtogether.title: How do I print words and a number together?

sections.p: There are two ways. Both give the same result.
Python adds a space between the pieces for you, and it works with any kind of value.
`+` only joins text to text. So a number has to be turned into text first with `str()`. You also have to type the space yourself.

sections.warn: `print("Whole minutes: " + 2)` crashes with a TypeError, because `+` can't join text and a number.

predict.title: How do I write a prediction?

sections.p: A **prediction** is your guess of what Python will show, written **before** you run the code. It makes you think first, and Python then tells you if you were right.

steps: Look at one line, like `print(7 // 2)`.
Work out the answer in your head or on paper.
Type your answer at the end of the line, after a few spaces: `print(7 // 2)   # my guess: 3`.
Do that for every line **before** you click Run.
Click Run and compare. If a guess was wrong, that's great: it means you learned something.

sections.good: Wrong guesses cost you nothing. The check only needs a comment on the line, so write your honest guess.

sections.p: Click **Run** one last time. Your program runs from top to bottom with **no red error**.

kn2.title: Your code has the comments (#) the steps asked for, and...

sections.p: Your code has the comments (`#`) the steps asked for, and **nothing was deleted**: earlier work is still there, commented out.
